summary: The build can start: required runtime (Node.js 24), MCP servers (documentdb, azure, learn) and DocumentDB agent skills are installed, and authoritative Microsoft Learn pages and installed skills verify the facts needed to build. However: the prompt requests Beanie (a Python ODM) together with Node.js — the builder must choose a Node.js ODM (for example Mongoose) or switch to Python, the local mongo shell (mongosh) is not installed (hand inspection / debugging tool), and a few cold answers were incorrect and must be corrected before coding (resource type, CLI group, billing model, connection-url patterns, vector-index syntax, integrated search, local gateway port).
summary_points: Build can begin: Node.js 24, npm/npx, docker, and the documentdb MCP server plus many documentdb-* skills are available to inspect and verify the live cluster.
Major prompt contradiction: Beanie is Python-only; the builder must either switch to Python (and use Beanie) or use a Node.js ODM (for example Mongoose).

Key service facts were wrong in the cold answers and have been verified against Microsoft Learn and installed skills (resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters; CLI group is az documentdb; billing is vCore/compute tiers, not RUs; connection strings use mongodb+srv with TLS and cluster-specific hostnames; DocumentDB provides integrated text & vector search).

Missing but useful developer tools: mongosh is not on PATH (hand-checks), and optional infra tools (bicep/terraform/azd) are not installed but not required for this sample because provisioning is disallowed by run policy.
Verdict is ready_with_gaps: proceed after resolving the ODM/language choice and optionally installing mongosh for manual verification.

tools.name: node
tools.needed_for: Run and develop the requested Node.js LangChain agent, npm installs, run scripts and npx.
tools.workaround: Switch the sample to Python (requires Python toolchain and ODM change).

tools.name: npx
tools.needed_for: Start MCP servers and install agent skills or run npx-based project commands.
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to run local npx utilities and MCP helper scripts.
tools.workaround: Install npx (npm install -g npx) or run scripts via npm scripts.

tools.name: npm / Node package tooling (implicit)
tools.needed_for: Install dependencies (mongodb, mongoose or alternative, langchain packages for Node, etc.).
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot install or run the sample.
tools.workaround: Install Node/npm; or convert to Python sample.

tools.name: documentdb MCP server (documentdb)
tools.needed_for: Data-plane inspection of the live DocumentDB cluster: list databases/collections, sample documents, create/list indexes, explain query plans, insert/update documents to verify the sample created collections and indexes.
tools.detail: 18 tools (list_databases, find_documents, create_index, explain_operation, etc.) — connection_profile 'default' to the cluster
tools.impact_if_missing: Can't programmatically inspect the live cluster from the agent to confirm what the sample created; manual portal checks would be needed.
tools.workaround: Use az / Azure portal to check the cluster or install the documentdb MCP server profile (mcp entry).

tools.name: learn (Microsoft Learn MCP server)
tools.needed_for: Search and fetch authoritative Microsoft Learn documentation to verify service facts and to ground cold answers.
tools.impact_if_missing: Agent would have no easy, authoritative Microsoft Learn grounding for service-specific facts.
tools.workaround: Use the Azure 'azure' MCP server (control-plane) or manually cite official docs, but learn is the fastest authoritative source.

tools.name: documentdb-* skills (documentdb-connection, documentdb-vector-search, documentdb-local-deployment, documentdb-indexing, documentdb-azure-deployment, ...)
tools.needed_for: Domain-specific guidance and examples: connection best practices, vector & search index examples and quickstarts, local gateway config, data-modeling and deployment guidance.
tools.detail: Multiple installed skills including documentdb-connection, documentdb-vector-search, documentdb-local-deployment, documentdb-indexing, documentdb-azure-deployment, etc.
tools.impact_if_missing: Loss of ready-made, authoritative agent guidance and templates for index creation, connection config, and local dev.
tools.workaround: Use Microsoft Learn pages and general MongoDB docs, but installed skills are tailored for Azure DocumentDB.

tools.name: docker
tools.needed_for: Run the local DocumentDB Gateway image for local development/testing if the builder chooses to run against a local gateway instead of the live cluster.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run local gateway; must use live cluster for verification.
tools.workaround: Use the live DocumentDB cluster reachable from this machine (DOCUMENTDB_URI) as the prompt instructs.

tools.name: python
tools.needed_for: If the builder decides to follow the prompt's Beanie ODM requirement, the sample must be implemented in Python and use the Python toolchain.
tools.impact_if_missing: If Beanie were mandatory and python missing, the build would be blocked.
tools.workaround: Substitute a Node.js ODM (Mongoose) and keep the Node.js runtime; or install Python.

tools.name: az (Azure CLI)
tools.needed_for: Inspect Azure resources and read control-plane properties (resource groups, check cluster properties, firewall rules, list connection strings), useful for read-only verification tasks.
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to query control-plane resource metadata from the CLI; could still use Azure portal.
tools.workaround: Use Azure portal or REST API to inspect resources.

tools.name: mongosh
tools.needed_for: Manual connectivity checks, one-off queries and index verification by hand on the DocumentDB cluster; useful for rapid local debugging and validation.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run interactive shell checks locally; every check must be done via the documentdb MCP server or the portal.
tools.workaround: Use the documentdb MCP server's find_documents / explain / list_indexes tools to inspect the live cluster; or install mongosh.

tools.name: azd
tools.needed_for: Optional: template-based project provisioning & deploy flows — NOT required for this sample (the run-environment forbids provisioning another cluster).
tools.impact_if_missing: No impact for a sample that uses an existing cluster; azd would only speed deployments.
tools.workaround: Use az CLI or manual instructions; do not provision additional clusters because run policy forbids Azure writes.

tools.name: bicep
tools.needed_for: Optional: authoring Bicep IaC for cluster deployment; not required because the sample must not provision a new cluster.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run bicep build locally; not required for this sample since no provisioning is allowed.
tools.workaround: Provide Bicep templates as text in the repo and instruct users to install Bicep if they want to deploy; or rely on az CLI examples.

tools.name: terraform
tools.needed_for: Optional: authoring Terraform infra; not required for this sample as provisioning is disallowed.
tools.impact_if_missing: No impact for sample building against existing cluster.
tools.workaround: Provide Terraform examples in repo and indicate how to install terraform for readers who want to provision.

tools.needed_for: Source control for the sample repository.
tools.impact_if_missing: Can't clone/push the sample repo locally.
tools.workaround: Use downloadable zip or scp of files.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type for an account: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (sub-resources include databaseAccounts/mongodbDatabases, databaseAccounts/mongodbCollections).
confusions.grounded_answer: The resource provider namespace is Microsoft.DocumentDB and the cluster resource type for the vCore-based managed MongoDB product is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not databaseAccounts).

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters 2024-07-01 (deployment-language-terraform)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Both Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU) historically used Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts and the namespaces are similar; older docs and templates still reference databaseAccounts, so the model produced the older Cosmos DB pattern.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder used Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts in ARM/Bicep or tried to call az cosmosdb commands, they would attempt the wrong control-plane API and possibly provision or inspect the wrong service type.
improvements: Rename or add a prominent note on the Microsoft Learn overview and quickstarts that vCore clusters use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (and show a Bicep/ARM snippet) to stop readers assuming databaseAccounts.
Add a deprecation/clarifying banner to older databaseAccounts templates indicating the new mongoClusters resource type for vCore DocumentDB.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the built-in az cosmosdb command group. Example to create a MongoDB API account: az cosmosdb create ... This is in the core az CLI (az cosmosdb).
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the az documentdb command group (for example az documentdb mongocluster create). The documentdb CLI group manages vCore-based Azure DocumentDB mongoClusters.

grounding_links.title: az documentdb mongocluster create
Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts) historically uses az cosmosdb and their command group is commonly used for Cosmos resources. The new vCore DocumentDB CLI group is az documentdb and the naming similarity caused the mix-up.

confusion_sources.title: az cosmosdb command group docs (older Cosmos DB guidance)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder used az cosmosdb commands they would operate against Cosmos DB control-plane resources, not the vCore DocumentDB clusters; CLI commands would fail or return unrelated resources.
improvements: Add a 'Which CLI group to use' section to the quickstart page that explicitly contrasts az documentdb (mongoClusters) vs az cosmosdb (databaseAccounts).
Update the Azure CLI docs to cross-link az documentdb examples when the product name 'DocumentDB' appears.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep: resource of type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts ... Terraform (azurerm): resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" ... kind = 'MongoDB'.
confusions.grounded_answer: The vCore DocumentDB cluster is deployed as Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (Bicep/ARM) and corresponding AzAPI/Terraform types reference Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters or the Azure Verified Module for Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore) / documentdb mongo cluster resources.

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (deployment-language-bicep)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB ARM/Bicep snippets used Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts; the vCore product adopted a new sub-resource type mongoClusters but the provider namespace is identical which causes confusion.
confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong ARM/Bicep resource type would mean the IaC would target Cosmos DB accounts or fail to deploy the desired mongoClusters resource.
improvements: Add explicit Bicep/ARM and Terraform examples on the quickstart for Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and mark older databaseAccounts examples as targeting Cosmos DB, not DocumentDB vCore.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: MongoDB-compatible connection string uses mongodb:// (SRV not always supported). Host looks like <account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com and the TLS port is 10255. Example: mongodb://<username>:<password>@myaccount.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retrywrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000&appName=@myaccount@ . Username is often formatted as '<dbuser>@<account>' for Cosmos DB; TLS/SSL=true is required.
confusions.grounded_answer: For vCore Azure DocumentDB clusters use the cluster SRV-style hostnames (mongodb+srv://) with host <cluster>.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com or <cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com and TLS enabled (tls=true). For non-SRV forms use the cluster's explicit host and recommended TLS options; port 10255 is typical for older Cosmos DB for MongoDB accounts but the vCore DocumentDB docs show customers should prefer mongodb+srv endpoints and the cluster-specific hostnames. Username/password forms differ from legacy Cosmos; role-based (Entra) flows use MONGODB-OIDC if used.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID
Connect a MongoDB application to Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer describes the older Cosmos DB MongoDB API connection string (documents.azure.com or mongo.cosmos.azure.com on port 10255). The new vCore DocumentDB clusters expose SRV endpoints on mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com and support OIDC / SRV patterns.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB connection string examples (legacy docs)

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong host suffix or port can result in connection failures or misapplied TLS/auth settings. Using mongodb:// without SRV when the cluster expects mongodb+srv can lead to missed global endpoints.
improvements: Document the recommended connection string patterns for DocumentDB prominently on the quickstart including examples for mongodb+srv (with TLS/OIDC examples) and a short note comparing to older Cosmos DB endpoints.
Add a 'preferred connection' snippet to the documentdb-connection skill with explicit example URIs for SRV and non-SRV forms.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Azure Cosmos DB (DocumentDB) is billed by Request Units (RUs) for throughput; you provision RU/s (manual or autoscale) or use serverless on supported accounts. The MongoDB API on Cosmos is RU-based rather than vCore tiers. (There are other Azure managed MongoDB offerings with vCore-style SKUs, but classic DocumentDB/Cosmos uses RUs.)
confusions.grounded_answer: For the vCore Azure DocumentDB product billing is by compute cluster tier (vCores and memory, e.g., M30) and storage, not Request Units (RUs). DocumentDB uses vCore compute tiers and per-shard storage; RUs apply to Azure Cosmos DB (RU) SKU, which is a different product.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB pricing explained
FAQ: How does Azure DocumentDB relate to Azure Cosmos DB?

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cosmos DB (RU) uses a RU model and older Microsoft messaging often refers to RU billing; the two services are similar in surface area (both MongoDB-compatible) so the model conflated them.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB RU billing documentation (legacy Cosmos guidance)

confusions.build_risk: Planning capacity or demo expectations based on RUs would produce incorrect cost/sizing decisions and could choose wrong APIs / indexes for the chosen SKU.
improvements: Add a prominent 'billing model' section to the DocumentDB quickstart that explicitly contrasts vCore-tier billing (DocumentDB) and RU billing (Cosmos DB) with examples.
Add a note to the deployment skill templates specifying the billing model for each resource type.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: MongoDB API primarily uses MongoDB SCRAM username/password credentials... Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) token-based authentication is supported for some Cosmos APIs (SQL/Gremlin) but historically not for the MongoDB API; for MongoDB you authenticate with SCRAM credentials.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports native SCRAM credentials and also supports Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC-based flows) for role-based access to clusters. Drivers can connect using the MONGODB-OIDC / MONGODB-OIDC (OIDC) flow or SRV-form URIs and use OIDC-managed identities; the docs provide example connection URIs for MONGODB-OIDC and guidance to use authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC and tls true.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID
documentdb-connection skill

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historically Cosmos DB's Mongo API lacked AAD/OIDC for Mongo; the vCore DocumentDB product added explicit Entra/OIDC support (MONGODB-OIDC) in docs, and older knowledge led the model to hedge toward SCRAM-only.

confusion_sources.title: Older notes saying MongoDB API lacked AAD support

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes only SCRAM credentials, they may not implement the recommended RBAC flows or managed-identity authentication paths for production, and may hard-code passwords instead of using Entra identities.
improvements: Add a short example on the quickstart showing both SCRAM and Microsoft Entra (MONGODB-OIDC) connection URI examples and how to obtain/use an OIDC token with a driver.
Document the recommended production option (Entra ID) with a sample using @azure/identity or managed identity flows.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the standard MongoDB drivers for your language (e.g., npm package 'mongodb' for Node.js, pymongo/motor for Python). There is no separate MongoDB-API-specific Azure SDK for application-level MongoDB operations; the Azure SDKs are for Cosmos control-plane and management. For MongoDB protocol operations use the official MongoDB driver.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use the standard MongoDB drivers for application-level access (for Node.js use the official npm 'mongodb' driver). Azure SDKs are for control-plane management; application-level operations should use MongoDB drivers or an ODM appropriate to the runtime (Mongoose for Node.js, Beanie for Python).

grounding_links.title: DocumentDB Connection Optimizer (skill)
Connect a MongoDB application to Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: n/a
confusions.build_risk: None if correct driver used; risk arises only from the Beanie/Node mismatch in prompt (Beanie is Python-only).

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: MongoDB-style vector indexes expose algorithms like HNSW and IVF (some providers also offer DiskANN). Example (MongoDB 7+ style): db.prescriptions.createIndex( { embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'emb_idx', vector: { algorithm: 'hnsw', similarity: 'cosine', m: 16, efConstruction: 200 } } );
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports vector index kinds: vector-hnsw, vector-ivf and vector-diskann (DiskANN recommended at scale). Indexes are created using DocumentDB's createIndexes/runCommand pattern with 'cosmosSearchOptions' or a 'kind' parameter, for example a JSON createIndexes command specifying kind:'vector-hnsw' or kind:'vector-diskann' and additional algorithm-specific parameters (m/efConstruction for HNSW, numLists for IVF, maxDegree/lBuild/lSearch for DiskANN).

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (vector-search)
Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (DiskANN/IVF docs)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used a MongoDB 7+ community-style createIndex shape; DocumentDB exposes a specialized createIndexes/command-style payload and different option names (cosmosSearchOptions / kind / vector-*), so syntax and param names differ.
confusions.build_risk: Using community MongoDB createIndex syntax would fail against DocumentDB or produce an index with wrong parameters. Index should be created using DocumentDB's createIndexes/cosmosSearch options to get DiskANN/HNSW/IVF behavior.
improvements: Add a short 'create vector index' snippet to the quickstart showing the exact createIndexes command with 'kind' and DiskANN/HNSW/IVF parameter names.
Expose the DocumentDB createIndex JSON templates in the documentdb-vector-search skill for copy/paste.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: There is no built-in Lucene-style full-text search in Cosmos's MongoDB API historically; use Azure Cognitive Search to index documents from Cosmos DB for full-text/hybrid search, or use application-side hybrid ranking that combines vector nearest-neighbour results from the vector index with keyword hits from Azure Cognitive Search.
confusions.grounded_answer: Incorrect for the vCore DocumentDB product: Azure DocumentDB includes integrated full-text search and a unified $search pipeline stage; you can create search indexes (BM25) and combine lexical (BM25) and vector retrieval (DiskANN/HNSW/IVF) within the same collection using the createSearchIndexes/createIndexes and the $search aggregation stage (cosmosSearch operator) for hybrid retrieval.

grounding_links.title: Full-text and hybrid search with createSearchIndexes and $search (DocumentDB)
documentdb-full-text-search (skill)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB MongoDB API lacked an integrated Lucene-style Search in some tiers; many authors used Azure Cognitive Search as an external index, so the model reflected that historic pattern instead of the current integrated DocumentDB search.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cognitive Search + Cosmos DB guidance (older patterns)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder omitted DocumentDB's integrated search and instead wired Azure Cognitive Search, they'd produce a more complex architecture and miss DocumentDB-native performance and index examples.
improvements: Prominently document integrated full-text & hybrid search in quickstarts and add an example that shows BM25 + vector fusion using the $search stage to avoid people defaulting to Azure Cognitive Search.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Supported wire protocol depends on the account configuration; modern managed MongoDB-compatible accounts may advertise support for up to MongoDB 7.0. However Cosmos DB historically lagged and supported older protocols; assume compatibility with many 4.x/5.x client features but verify the account's advertised wire protocol. Commonly-missing features: some server-side JavaScript, certain admin/diagnostic commands, full replica-set control, and advanced sharding/transactions features may be limited or behave differently.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore) documents state support for MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 (explicitly supported). Some admin-level commands and provider-specific features may differ; DocumentDB implements ~99% of MongoDB operators but administrative commands and certain server internals are not exposed. Builders should verify specific MQL/command compatibility with the migration assessment or compatibility docs.

grounding_links.title: FAQ and compatibility notes (supported wire protocol versions)
MongoDB compatibility and feature coverage

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: General statements about Cosmos DB lagging produced a cautious answer; the current vCore DocumentDB explicitly supports modern wire protocol versions and documents coverage.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumed an older wire protocol, they might pick incompatible driver versions or features; conversely, assuming full admin parity with plain mongod could cause runtime errors.
improvements: Add a single compatibility table on the quickstart listing supported wire versions and a short 'what's not supported' checklist with examples of known admin commands that are not exposed.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: There is no full local emulator for the Cosmos DB MongoDB API. For development run an official MongoDB docker image (match the advertised server version, e.g. mongo:7.0) and connect to it on the standard port 27017 (mongodb://localhost:27017). For Cosmos DB-specific behavior there is an Azure Cosmos DB Emulator but it has historically supported only the SQL (Core) API, not the MongoDB API.
confusions.grounded_answer: Incorrect for DocumentDB: there is a DocumentDB Gateway Docker image intended for local development (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local) exposing the MongoDB wire protocol on port 10260 (and PostgreSQL on 9712) with TLS and SCRAM-SHA-256; use the gateway Docker image for a local dev/test environment to better match DocumentDB behavior.

grounding_links.title: documentdb-local-deployment (skill)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer assumed the lack of an emulator (true for older Cosmos DB Mongo API), and advised using a standard mongo: image; the DocumentDB project provides a specialized gateway image and documented port (10260).
confusions.build_risk: If the builder ran a plain mongo: container they would miss DocumentDB-specific behaviors (vector search, integrated text search, DocumentDB admin features and ports) and tests could give false confidence.
improvements: Add a 'local gateway' quickstart README section with the exact docker-compose YAML and the recommended local connection flags (TLS, tlsAllowInvalidCertificates for local only), and publish the gateway image name prominently in quickstarts.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change streams require a replica-set-like topology and MongoDB 3.6+ wire protocol. If the managed service advertises full MongoDB change stream support (MongoDB API on some providers does), you can use them without extra account-level toggles other than correct user privileges. For Cosmos DB specifically, change-stream-like functionality exists as the Change Feed for core/SQL API; MongoDB change streams support has historically been limited or absent—verify on the account. If supported, no special flag beyond appropriate user privileges is normally required.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports change streams and they are used for online migrations and triggers; migration docs and function triggers reference enabling change streams on the source or ensuring the source supports them. For DocumentDB itself, change-stream-based triggers and the change-stream feature are available and used by migration tools; consult the migration docs for any source-specific enablement steps.

grounding_links.title: Migrate from other MongoDB-compatible services to Azure DocumentDB (change-stream guidance)
Azure DocumentDB trigger for Azure Functions (uses change streams)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model mixed older Cosmos DB limitations with the vCore DocumentDB's current migration and change-stream support; historically some managed services lacked standard change stream support, causing ambiguity.

confusion_sources.title: Change Feed for Cosmos DB core SQL API (often confused with Mongo change streams)

confusions.build_risk: Assuming change streams are not available would force the builder to use offline migration paths or polling, adding complexity and longer migration windows.
improvements: Add a short 'change streams' section in the migration quickstart explaining how DocumentDB supports them and any account settings to review.
Include a code snippet that shows how to read change streams from a DocumentDB collection with a Node.js driver.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the 'documentdb' MCP server (the service-specific MCP server) for data-plane inspection and tools; the general Azure MCP server covers control-plane management (resources) but the 'documentdb' server supplies MongoDB/Cosmos-specific inspection commands (collections, indexes, query plans).
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the documentdb MCP server provides data-plane tools (list/index/aggregate/explain) and the azure MCP server covers control-plane tasks and best-practice lookups.

grounding_links.title: documentdb MCP server (inventory)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: n/a
confusions.build_risk: None; documentdb MCP is available per inventory.

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: The name 'DocumentDB' was the original name of Microsoft's Azure DocumentDB service which later evolved into Azure Cosmos DB. Cosmos DB is the multi-model, globally distributed successor and hosts multiple APIs including a MongoDB-compatible API. This Microsoft DocumentDB/Cosmos DB is distinct from any unrelated open-source project named 'DocumentDB'.
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly correct but incomplete: the original Azure DocumentDB brand was the precursor to Azure Cosmos DB. More recently Microsoft introduced a separate vCore-based product called Azure DocumentDB (distinct from Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU)), aligned with the open-source DocumentDB engine. In short: (a) old 'DocumentDB' → became Cosmos DB; (b) the new vCore Azure DocumentDB is a different offering (previously called 'vCore-based Cosmos DB for MongoDB') and is allied with the open-source DocumentDB engine.

grounding_links.title: Compare Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB Atlas (notes on naming and relation)
FAQ: relation to Azure Cosmos DB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The historical name 'DocumentDB' and the evolution to Cosmos DB plus the introduction of a separate vCore product named DocumentDB cause overlapping terminology.

confusion_sources.title: Older blog posts and docs that equate 'DocumentDB' with Cosmos DB

confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses 'DocumentDB' without clarifying which product (the historic Cosmos DB vs the new vCore offering), they may pick wrong APIs, CLI groups, or resource types.
improvements: Add a short 'names & products' table at the top of the product landing page clarifying that 'Azure Cosmos DB (RU)' is distinct from the vCore 'Azure DocumentDB' product and list which resource types/CLI groups correspond to each.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Under the MongoDB API the underlying engine is the managed service's proprietary storage engine (Cosmos DB's engine or the provider's managed engine), not a vanilla mongod process. It implements the MongoDB wire protocol so most MongoDB drivers and application code work unchanged, but certain server-side features, admin commands, and performance characteristics differ. Expect to use standard MongoDB drivers but avoid relying on unsupported server internals or admin commands.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore) is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine (the project 'DocumentDB') rather than a stock mongod process. The service implements the MongoDB wire protocol for application compatibility so most MongoDB drivers and application code remain unchanged, but certain admin commands or provider internals differ and should not be relied upon.

grounding_links.title: Moving from another MongoDB-compatible service to Azure DocumentDB (engine details)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described a generic 'managed proprietary' engine which captures some providers; the product docs explicitly name the open-source DocumentDB engine as the basis for vCore DocumentDB.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming a mongod process under the hood may lead a builder to rely on admin commands not available on DocumentDB; however application-level code using MongoDB drivers generally works.
improvements: Add a short sentence in the quickstart: 'DocumentDB vCore is powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine; drivers work but admin operations differ.'

confusions.question: What connection string env var and exact DB name should the sample read and use?
confusions.cold_answer: Read the MongoDB-compatible connection string from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime. Use the database name sample_healthcare_15 for all sample collections/operations.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the sample-run environment instructs the app to read the cluster connection string from DOCUMENTDB_URI and to use the database sample_healthcare_15.

grounding_links.title: DocumentDB Connection Optimizer (skill)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: n/a
confusions.build_risk: None.

confusions.question: What vector index definition will this sample create for embeddings?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a vector index on the embedding field using the MongoDB createIndex vector syntax. Example: db.prescriptions.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'emb_idx', vector: { algorithm: 'hnsw', similarity: 'cosine', m: 16, efConstruction: 200 } }) — tune m/efConstruction per the cluster's documented limits.
confusions.grounded_answer: DocumentDB requires createIndexes via the admin/command form with algorithm-specific options; supported kinds are vector-hnsw, vector-ivf and vector-diskann and the index is created with the 'kind' or 'cosmosSearchOptions' parameters (see vector-search quickstarts). The sample should create, e.g., a DiskANN index for production-scale or HNSW for small demos using the DocumentDB createIndexes payload.

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used generic MongoDB 7+ createIndex vector syntax; DocumentDB uses its own createIndexes/cosmosSearchOptions shape and option names.
confusions.build_risk: Using the generic createIndex syntax will either fail or not produce the intended DocumentDB optimized index; must use DocumentDB index creation examples.
improvements: Publish a copy/paste createIndexes JSON example for the sample's embedding dims and algorithm (DiskANN/HNSW/IVF) in the repo and the documentdb-vector-search skill.

confusions.question: What exact port and TLS settings will the sample use to connect?
confusions.cold_answer: Connect over TLS to port 10255 (mongodb://...:10255) and include ssl=true (or tls=true) in the connection string query options. Example client URI: mongodb://user:pass@host:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb
confusions.grounded_answer: DocumentDB quickstarts recommend using SRV (mongodb+srv) endpoints with TLS enabled (tls=true) and cluster hostnames on the mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com domain; the older Cosmos DB for MongoDB used port 10255. For local DocumentDB Gateway (dev), the local gateway listens on port 10260 (with TLS and self-signed certs). Use SRV endpoints (no explicit port) for production cluster URIs and follow DocumentDB docs for TLS and OIDC options.

confusions.question: Which client library will the Node.js app use to talk to the service?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the official Node.js MongoDB driver (npm install mongodb) to connect to the MongoDB-compatible endpoint. For ODM behavior use a MongoDB-compatible ODM (Mongoose) on Node—(Beanie is a Python ODM; do not mix languages).
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the app should use the official Node.js MongoDB driver (npm 'mongodb') for driver-level operations. For ODM in Node.js, use Mongoose or another Node ODM. If Beanie is required, the builder must change the implementation language to Python.

confusions.question: What MCP command pattern will I use to inspect collections/indexes and query plans?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the documentdb MCP server profile (default) with commands that map to collection/index inspection. Example pattern: mcp documentdb collections list --profile default --database sample_healthcare_15 and mcp documentdb indexes show --profile default --database sample_healthcare_15 --collection prescriptions. (Exact mcp subcommand names depend on the installed MCP tool; adjust if necessary.)
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the documentdb MCP server (inventory) provides commands for listing databases/collections, listing indexes and running explain; use the documentdb profile (connection_profile 'default') and the server's tools (documentdb_list_databases, documentdb_list_indexes, documentdb_explain_operation, etc.) to inspect the live cluster.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Do not use Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts or the az cosmosdb CLI group to create or manage the vCore DocumentDB cluster; use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and the az documentdb mongocluster commands instead.

Don't plan capacity or billing using Request Units (RUs); size the sample for vCore cluster tiers (M10/M20/M30 etc.) and storage, because Azure DocumentDB (vCore) is billed by compute tier (vCores) and storage.

Use the standard MongoDB Node.js driver (npm 'mongodb') for application access; if you must remain in Node.js use a Node ODM such as Mongoose instead of Beanie (Beanie is Python-only); alternatively reimplement the sample in Python to use Beanie.
